chapters.title: Chapter 3: How Policy Flows Into Asset Prices

lessons.title: Bonds First: Why G-Sec Yields React Before Anything Else

body.text: When the RBI speaks, the government bond market answers first, often within seconds. Every other interest rate in India, from corporate bonds to FDs to home loans, is priced as a spread over government bond yields. Learn to read G-Sec yields and you can see where borrowing costs are heading weeks or months before your bank tells you.

children.text: Chapters 1 and 2 covered what the RBI is and the tools it uses. Chapter 3 follows those tools out into the markets you actually invest in. We start with the market that moves first and matters most: government securities.
What a G-Sec Actually Is

markDefs.definition: A bond issued by the Government of India, or a state government, to borrow money. Short-term ones under a year are Treasury Bills; longer ones are dated securities.

children.text: A
government security (G-Sec)

is an IOU from the Government of India. You lend money today; the government pays you fixed interest every six months and returns your money at maturity. Short-term borrowing of 91, 182 or 364 days uses Treasury Bills; longer borrowing uses dated securities of up to 40 years or more.

markDefs.definition: The fixed annual interest a bond pays, expressed as a percentage of its face value. Indian G-Secs pay it in two equal half-yearly instalments.
The annual return an investor earns if they buy a bond at today's market price and hold it to maturity, including coupons and any gain or loss on the price.

children.text: Take the current 10-year benchmark, the
. It has a face value of ₹100 and a
coupon

of 6.94%, so it pays ₹6.94 a year, in two instalments of ₹3.47, until it matures in 2036. The coupon never changes. What changes every second is the price investors are willing to pay for it, and therefore its
yield
The Seesaw: Why Prices Fall When Yields Rise

Imagine you own that 6.94% bond. Tomorrow, interest rates in the economy rise, and new 10-year bonds pay 7.44%. Nobody will pay you ₹100 for a bond paying 6.94% when they can get 7.44% elsewhere. To sell, you must cut the price until your bond also yields 7.44% to a new buyer.

body.caption: A quick approximation. The full yield to maturity also counts the gain or loss between today's price and the ₹100 repaid at maturity.

children.text: If the bond's price drops to ₹98, its current yield becomes 6.94 ÷ 98 × 100 = 7.08%. Price down, yield up. They always move in opposite directions.

body.caption: The 6.94% GS 2036: Price at Different Market Yields (10 years to maturity, half-yearly coupons)

body.title: Complete the Rule
body.textWithBlank: When bond yields rise, bond prices ___.
body.explanation: Prices fall. A bond's coupon is fixed, so the only way an existing bond can offer a higher yield to a new buyer is by becoming cheaper.

children.text: Why Bonds React Before Anything Else
Bonds are pure interest rate instruments.
A stock's value depends on earnings, management and a hundred other things. A G-Sec's value depends almost entirely on interest rates, so any change in rate expectations hits its price directly.
Professional traders react in seconds.
Bank treasuries, primary dealers and bond funds watch every RBI word live and trade the government bond market electronically as the statement is read.
Banks own a huge share of G-Secs.
Because banks hold government bonds for SLR and liquidity, a move in yields changes the value of their investment books immediately.
Everything else is priced off G-Secs.
Corporate bonds, commercial paper, FD rates and loan rates are all set as a spread over government yields, so they follow, but with a lag.

children.text: Duration: How Much a Bond Moves

markDefs.definition: An estimate of how much a bond's price changes, in percent, for a 1 percentage point change in its yield. Longer maturity and lower coupons mean higher duration.

children.text: Not all bonds move equally. A 91-day Treasury Bill barely moves when yields change, because you get your money back in three months. A 30-year bond can swing sharply. The measure of this sensitivity is
modified duration

body.latex: \% \text{ change in price} \approx -\text{Modified duration} \times \text{Change in yield (percentage points)}
body.caption: The minus sign captures the seesaw: yields up, prices down

body.title: What Happens to a Gilt Fund?
body.prompt: A gilt mutual fund has a modified duration of 8 years. After hawkish RBI signals, the yields on its bonds rise by 25 basis points. Approximately what percentage change should you expect in the fund's NAV? Enter a negative number for a fall.
body.explanation: Change ≈ −8 × 0.25 = -2%. A ₹1,00,000 investment would drop by about ₹2,000 on this move alone, before counting the coupon income the fund keeps earning. That is why long-duration debt funds are hit hardest when the RBI turns hawkish, and gain most when it turns dovish.

body.caption: How Rate-Sensitive Are Common Debt Fund Categories?

cells: A few days to about 3 months

children.text: The Yield Curve: Reading the Market's Forecast

markDefs.definition: A line connecting yields of government bonds of different maturities. Its slope shows what markets expect for future interest rates and inflation.

children.text: Plot yields across maturities and you get the
yield curve
. The short end is anchored by the RBI's policy rate. The long end reflects what markets expect for inflation, growth and future policy over many years.

The curve today slopes steeply upward: about 5.2% at three months and near 7% at ten years. Part of that gap is normal, since investors want extra return for lending longer. But a steep rise like this also tells you the market expects inflation to climb and sees a real chance of RBI rate hikes ahead.

columns.label: Steep upward curve
points: Long yields well above short yields
Markets expect higher inflation or future rate hikes
Common when a central bank is seen as behind the curve on inflation

columns.label: Flat or inverted curve
points: Long yields close to or below short yields
Markets expect rate cuts or slowing growth ahead
Often seen late in a hiking cycle
In the US, an inversion has often come before recessions

children.text: Case 1: Bonds Moved Before the RBI Did, 2022
In early 2022, the repo rate was still at a record low of 4% and the RBI had not hiked. But inflation was running above 6%, and bond traders did not wait for permission.

events.title: 10-year yield hits 6.52%
events.description: A two-year high, with the repo rate still at 4.00%. Markets were already pricing in tighter policy.

events.title: Off-cycle RBI hike
events.description: The RBI finally moved, raising the repo rate by 40 basis points to 4.40% at an unscheduled meeting.

events.title: 10-year yield reaches 7.53%
events.description: The highest since March 2019, a day before the RBI's next decision, as traders priced in a big hike.

events.title: RBI hikes 50 bps to 4.90%
events.description: The RBI delivered roughly what the bond market had already priced in.

body.text: The 10-year yield hit a two-year high in January 2022, four months before the RBI's first hike, and was already near its peak before the June decision. If you want an early warning of where rates are heading, watch the bond market, not the headlines.

children.text: Case 2: Yields Rising With the Repo Rate Unchanged, 2026

The repo rate has been 5.25% since December 2025. Yet the 10-year yield, which began 2026 around 6.6%, was near 7% by mid-September 2026. The benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond touched 7.02% during trading, its highest level in more than three months.

What pushed yields up without any RBI rate move? Everything you have studied so far: the RBI projecting CPI inflation to peak at 5.9%, the hawkish August minutes, OMO sales draining liquidity, and Brent crude near $97 a barrel adding to inflation fears.

body.title: Measure the Spread
body.prompt: On 11 September 2026, the 10-year G-Sec closed at about 6.96% and the repo rate was 5.25%. What is the spread between them, in basis points?
body.explanation: 6.96% minus 5.25% = 1.71 percentage points = 171 basis points. In June 2025 the gap was 79 basis points (6.29% minus 5.50%). A widening spread with an unchanged repo rate is the bond market saying it expects the next policy move to be up, not down.

body.title: Why Did Yields Rise?
body.question: Between January and September 2026, the repo rate stayed at 5.25% but the 10-year yield rose from about 6.6% to near 7%. What is the best explanation?
options: The RBI secretly raised the repo rate
Markets began pricing in higher inflation and possible future rate hikes
Government bonds became riskier because India might default
Banks were forced to sell all their bonds by law
body.explanation: Long-term yields reflect expected future rates and inflation, not just today's repo rate. Rising inflation projections, hawkish MPC minutes, higher oil prices and OMO sales all pointed to tighter policy ahead, so bond investors demanded higher yields now.

children.text: Who Is on the Other Side of the Trade?

body.title: Who Owned India's Central Government Securities, End-March 2024 (%)

data.label: RBI, mutual funds, FPIs and others

children.text: Banks and insurers dominate. Banks need G-Secs for SLR and liquidity; insurers and pension funds need long-dated, safe assets to match promises they make to policyholders decades away. That is why the bond market reacts so professionally, and so quickly, to the RBI.

events.description: India joined with a projected weight of about 9.35%, second only to China.

events.description: Despite the government removing capital gains and withholding tax on foreign investment in G-Secs on 5 June 2026, Bloomberg postponed inclusion in its flagship index.

body.text: Foreign investors still own only a small slice of India's government bonds: fully accessible route securities held by FPIs were about ₹3.75 lakh crore, or 3.34% of outstanding G-Secs, in May 2026. But because they trade actively and react to global events, their flows can move yields and the rupee far more than their share suggests.

body.title: Go Deeper: How the Government Actually Borrows

children.text: The government announces a borrowing calendar for each half of the financial year.
The RBI, as the government's debt manager, conducts weekly auctions of dated securities and Treasury Bills.
Banks, primary dealers, insurers and others bid; non-competitive bids from small investors are allotted at the auction's average price.
Once issued, the bonds trade in the secondary market, mainly on the RBI's electronic NDS-OM platform.
State governments borrow the same way through State Development Loans, which usually yield a little more than central G-Secs of similar maturity.

body.title: FD or Gilt Fund Right Now?
body.scenario: It is September 2026. A 5-year bank FD offers 6.75%. A gilt fund with a modified duration of 8 years holds bonds yielding about 7%. Inflation is projected to peak at 5.9% in October to December, and markets are pricing in a possible RBI rate hike. Your cousin wants to invest ₹5 lakh for five years and asks which is better.
body.prompt: Compare the two options given the current rate outlook. What would you tell your cousin?
body.modelAnswer: The FD locks in 6.75% for five years with no price risk, and deposit insurance covers up to ₹5 lakh per bank. The gilt fund offers a slightly higher running yield of about 7%, but its NAV moves with yields. If the RBI hikes and yields rise another 50 basis points, the fund could lose about 4% in value in the short run (−8 × 0.50), wiping out more than half a year of income. Over a full five years, higher yields would eventually be earned on reinvested bonds, but the ride would be bumpy. If yields instead fall later in the cycle, the fund would gain. So the honest answer depends on your cousin's tolerance for short-term swings. For someone who wants certainty, the FD, or a shorter-duration debt fund, is more sensible right now. A gilt fund suits an investor who can sit through temporary losses and believes yields are closer to their peak than their bottom. Taxes also matter: FD interest and debt fund gains are both taxed at slab rates for investments made after April 2023.

cards.definition: A bond issued by the government. Treasury Bills are under one year; dated securities are longer.
The fixed annual interest a bond pays as a percentage of its ₹100 face value.
The return you earn buying a bond at today's price and holding it to maturity.
Bond prices and yields always move in opposite directions.
The approximate percentage change in a bond's price for a 1 percentage point change in yield.
Yields plotted across maturities; its slope shows expected future rates and inflation.
The most actively traded G-Sec of a maturity, such as the 6.94% GS 2036 for 10 years, used as the market reference.

body.label: RBI Retail Direct
body.description: Launched in November 2021, this RBI portal lets individuals open a gilt account and buy Treasury Bills, dated G-Secs and State Development Loans directly, without a broker.

body.title: Build Your Bond Market Habit
steps: Look up today's 10-year G-Sec yield and note the benchmark bond's name
Find the latest 91-day Treasury Bill cut-off yield and compare it with the 5.25% repo rate
Sketch the yield curve with the 91-day, 5-year and 10-year yields and describe its slope
Check the modified duration of any debt fund you own on its monthly factsheet
On the next RBI policy day, check the 10-year yield within an hour of the announcement

points: G-Sec prices and yields move in opposite directions, and government bond yields are the base on which every other interest rate in India is priced.
Bonds react first to the RBI because they are pure interest rate instruments, traded instantly by professional institutions.
Modified duration tells you how much a bond or debt fund moves: roughly minus duration times the change in yield.
The yield curve shows the market's forecast; in September 2026 it slopes steeply up, from about 5.2% at three months to near 7% at ten years.
In 2022 the 10-year yield rose to 7.53% before the RBI's June hike; in 2026 it climbed towards 7% with the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%.
Banks and insurers dominate G-Sec ownership, while foreign investors hold a small but influential share after India joined global bond indices.

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. Yields are approximate and as reported up to mid-September 2026. Bond price examples assume a simplified 10-year maturity. Fund duration ranges are indicative; always check the fund's factsheet.
